item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-latentspace-一场著名的虚拟细胞竞赛爆冷-线性模型打平了多数深度模型/
item.description: A top virtual cell competition proved that simple linear regression can match many deep learning models—the problem is not insufficient data information, but flawed evaluation metrics and training objectives themselves.
item.content:encoded:
A top virtual cell competition proved that simple linear regression can match many deep learning models—the problem is not insufficient data information, but flawed evaluation metrics and training objectives themselves.

High information density: from the virtual cell competition's upset to concrete numbers on Germany's biotech startup ecosystem, for anyone wanting to understand the real progress in this space—though you can skip the guest's opening minutes of modest preamble.

2:13 Virtual cell interest is heating up because of sequencing throughput, not algorithmic breakthroughs
Biohub just announced an $1.8 billion collaboration with DOE, NIH, Meta, and Google to generate the multi-scale biological data needed for next-generation virtual cells. Fabian sees the industry's renewed interest in virtual cells driven first and foremost by the explosion in data generation scale, not algorithmic breakthroughs—though he warns that many projects are just ‘slapping an AI label on themselves’ rather than actually solving the cell-type-specific screening problem pharma needs.

6:25 One experiment measured 10 million transcriptomes
Past perturbation experiments had far more cell types than perturbation conditions—typically just ‘control vs disease’ sparse comparisons. Parse Bio's giga lab measured 10 million transcriptomes in a single run; now hundreds of cell lines and thousands of drugs are tested in full perturbation combinations simultaneously, making the perturbation space as rich as the cell space for the first time—and that's what finally gives large-scale perturbation prediction models something real to work with.

16:21 Inductive bias doesn't improve prediction; data has the final say
On whether to add manual priors (inductive bias) to models for interpretability and robustness, Fabian's stance is clear: the literature repeatedly shows that too-strong priors sacrifice predictive power. He cites AlphaFold—early versions laboriously hand-coded the molecule's rotational invariance, but later versions let the model learn that symmetry from more data, and they became more flexible and effective. Long-term, models that rely more on data and less on manual constraints will win out; interpretability can only be added after the fact.

20:56 Virtual cells' bottleneck is the training objective, not the data
Early foundation model papers didn't seriously demonstrate scaling laws, which is why simple models could match them. But on harder tasks (like NicheFormer requiring prediction of a neighbor cell's state from one cell's expression), nonlinear models show real advantages. Fabian's scConcept model now scales to 350 million cells, about 100 million parameters, covers 16 species, and shows clear scaling behavior—proving the information is in the data, but prior training objectives and representations weren't truly leveraging it.

26:11 The virtual cell challenge upset: linear models matched many deep learning models
Arc Institute's Virtual Cell Challenge was like a cold splash: on basic tasks like cell type prediction, logistic regression was nearly optimal; on perturbation prediction, many ‘fancy’ deep models didn't clearly beat simple linear ones. The championship solution used flow matching and similar nonlinear methods, proving complex models help on harder tasks—but the competition's fixed metrics let participants game the leaderboard, so the Open Problems consortium now requires teams to submit additional evaluation metrics to truly expose model differences.

33:39 Germany's startups don't lack early capital; they lack risk-bearing later-stage VCs
Fabian thinks Germany and Europe have no shortage of early-stage funding (early VC, non-dilutive grants)—new EU startups now match US numbers, and Munich is Europe's hub for startup numbers. But when you get to larger bets like Series B, European VC clearly lags; many teams turn to US capital, which is Europe's most obvious fault line in deep tech.

38:59 Most ‘virtual cell platform’ companies quietly end up making drugs
Fabian sees a pattern repeat: many companies claiming to ‘decode biology’ and ‘build virtual cell platforms’ get big funding but can't clearly explain the business model, so eventually they pivot to ‘we're making drugs’—because investors understand that story better. By contrast, he sees Noetic taking a more solid path—moat isn't just the model but unique perturbation data generation, like their Cancer Organoid Perturbation Atlas co-built with pharma partners willing to pay directly for early data access.

46:42 Let models reverse-engineer the experiments you should run
Fabian's team's new Lab Compass is an inverse generative model: given a forward world model, it reverse-engineers what lab work you need to hit a target cell state. The team has run three or four ‘experiment-model-experiment’ fast loops with a Cambridge collaborator doing hematopoiesis research, though Fabian admits the full loop is still far from robot automation—mostly active learning for now, with the ultimate goal of pulling experiments into a reinforcement learning loop.

item.title: Nobody runs randomized controlled trials for educational products because proving they work doesn't make money
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-fromourneurons-教育产品没人做随机对照试验-因为验证了也不赚钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-fromourneurons-教育产品没人做随机对照试验-因为验证了也不赚钱/
item.description: Schools adopt teaching materials based on sales pitches, not evidence: no regulatory requirement for effectiveness, no profit in proving one product beats another, therefore no company will fund validation.
item.content:encoded:
Schools adopt teaching materials based on sales pitches, not evidence: no regulatory requirement for effectiveness, no profit in proving one product beats another, therefore no company will fund validation.

Information density is moderate; core value lies in two segments—the missing evidence framework in education and how tenure incentives suppress collaboration. The autism research and AI segments include concrete details, but the whole reads more like a roundtable conversation than a hard-hitting discovery.

7:14 Educational adoption runs on salesmanship because efficacy proof generates no profit
Jason Yeatman pointed out that schools use teaching materials and interventions primarily through sales representatives pitching to teachers and district leaders, with no regulatory requirement to prove effectiveness and no systematic comparison of teaching methods to identify the best approach. He stated directly that a large-scale randomized controlled trial costs enormous sums, and if the results don't generate profit, no company will fund validation of whether their product actually works. This isn't a failure of teachers or schools—it's a system-level gap: there's no mechanism to bring scientific evidence into the purchasing process.

10:30 Academics chase first authorship; parents want their child helped—these goals diverge
Karen Parker traced the root of cross-institutional collaboration barriers to misaligned incentives: academics prioritize first authorship and all trial outcomes; parents care only about their own child. She noted that physics adopted a 'working group' model three decades ago—detailed contribution statements replacing author-order disputes. Neuroscience still lacks a solution for equitable credit distribution in large-team collaborations.

12:10 Career stage determines whether researchers can actually collaborate across disciplines
Karen Parker explained how career stage gates cooperation: junior researchers must chase first authorship; at promotion, they compete for last authorship; only after tenure as full professor does the pressure vanish, finally enabling their best cross-disciplinary work. The academic promotion system actually suppresses collaboration in its early stages—trainees can't really collaborate unless the incentive structure changes first.

14:30 Build trust with schools first by solving their real problems, research partnerships follow
Jason Yeatman described his playbook for school partnerships: don't enter asking teachers to make time for your research questions. Instead, deliver a tool they need immediately that solves their real problem, embedded in direct service. Once trust is built, schools open up to research questions. Many of his graduate students and postdocs found their research directions reshaped by real problems schools brought to them—for example, how to interpret assessments for English-language learners.

20:02 Autism research stumbles over sensory barriers and extreme participant diversity
Karen Parker outlined challenges in autism research that don't appear in typical-development studies. Many children's sensory sensitivities make brain imaging scans impossible; extensive family preparation is required beforehand. More difficult: age spans from three to seventeen years but requires a single outcome measure. The autism population is extremely heterogeneous—the same cohort might include both children with intellectual disability and a child with an IQ of 150, making trial design extraordinarily complex.

21:57 A shared registry compressed autism recruitment from years to six weeks
Karen Parker described how Simons Foundation's Spark project—a national autism family registry—compressed recruitment timelines. Recruiting hundreds used to cost approximately $5,000,000 and take years. Now a single survey-based questionnaire draws thousands of responses in six weeks, and the system directly routes families to trials matching their clinical criteria, dramatically accelerating research.

23:10 A reading assessment platform serving 1.2 million students has become a ready-made research cohort
Jason Yeatman explained that his reading assessment platform now serves approximately 1.2 million students across nearly 3,000 schools in daily use, accumulating continuous longitudinal data. He aspires to make it foundational infrastructure: the next generation of students and postdocs won't need to build cohorts from scratch but can pose the most important research questions. If they want to study high schoolers, years of data from elementary school forward may already be in hand.

25:18 AI can fabricate references so perfectly they'll pass funding review
Karen Parker shared a real lesson: a colleague used AI at 2 a.m. to draft a funding application; the AI-generated references were complete with journal, volume, and page numbers—all fabricated. Her conclusion: AI is a powerful research tool but can't replace thinking. Jason Yeatman added that he and his daughter built an interactive math website combining open-source curriculum with AI programming, but as a researcher he's more concerned that AI in education is advancing too fast with no mechanism in place to measure its effects.

item.title: Answers have become cheaper; what's truly scarce is the courage to commit to a bet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-zhixing-答案越来越便宜-真正稀缺的是选一个下注的勇气/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-zhixing-答案越来越便宜-真正稀缺的是选一个下注的勇气/
item.description: Shaonan believes that AI has made answers readily available, but what people really face is not information scarcity, but whether they dare to choose one possibility, commit to a bet, and then give their time to it in the face of infinite possibilities.
item.content:encoded:
Shaonan believes that AI has made answers readily available, but what people really face is not information scarcity, but whether they dare to choose one possibility, commit to a bet, and then give their time to it in the face of infinite possibilities.

If you find it convenient to ask AI questions but still don't know what to learn or what to believe in, this episode shifts the question from ‘what tool should I learn’ back to ‘what exactly do I want to commit my bet to’.

11:37 The opposite of anxiety is not calm, it's commitment
At twenty, you have countless possible lives ahead. If you keep holding onto those possibilities without committing, and drag on until forty still choosing, still waiting—what exactly are you waiting for? Shaonan's judgment is this: anxiety should point toward a concrete problem or direction. First figure out what you actually want to do, what problem you want to solve, then discuss whether and what you should learn. No one can answer your core question for you—not even AI.

19:31 AI is a tool that pulls you back toward the average
Large language models answer questions by predicting the probability of the next word—essentially an average calculated from vast amounts of text, the greatest common denominator of human thought. Much of the anxiety, Shaonan argues, comes from measuring yourself against an external yardstick that grows more anxiety-inducing the more you measure, because that yardstick was never meant for you. What you need to do is strive to escape these averages, find your own outlier point, and not expect AI to hand it to you.

23:02 AI flavor is the gap between taste and capability
Why do most people hate ‘AI flavor’—that telltale AI-generated quality? Our taste in things now far exceeds our actual ability to produce them, while AI can only produce average-level output: no point of view, no lived experience, either rehashing things everyone knows or speculating without detail. A simple test: read aloud what AI wrote. Language and text have their limits; accurately describing a song is far more complex than just listening to it.

30:55 What's worth recording is not knowledge, it's yourself
General knowledge no longer needs to be memorized by rote. Knowing about knowledge doesn't matter; knowing how to apply it does. What's worth recording is your thinking process: why a piece of knowledge matters, what views it corrected, what insight it gave you, how it connects to you. Even just excerpting a line—if you first tell it to yourself in your own words, you've truly thought it through. That act of investing attention is the value itself.

38:08 Reading's value is in attention, not the book itself
If AI can cover a book in five minutes, what's the point of reading? Shaonan's answer: it's not that reading is inherently better; it's that human attention works this way—the results are proportional to the attention you invest. Reading requires a sustained commitment of attention over time. The examples and ideas in a book that aren't directly aimed at your goal are often what spark new thinking. Spending the same time asking AI repeated questions about a topic could yield equally rich returns—what matters isn't the tool, but how much attention you bring and what goal you bring it to.

48:23 Each week, have AI recommend only three pieces of information
Shaonan offers a specific filtering method to push back against algorithmic spoon-feeding. The baseline: no recommendations from the past six months. First, news: using Hamming's ‘You and Your Research’ lens—are you working on the most important problem in your field?—have AI recommend one news item based on that. Second, a paper, and require AI to explain why it's worth reading. Third, high-entropy content: recommend something tangentially related (but not directly) to your usual discussion direction, perhaps art or design, to push back against fragmented information consumption.

1:04:58 The point of learning well: you still get to choose
Humans have infinite choices but cannot choose how they are born. Yet at every moment, even when not actively choosing, they're still making a choice, developing toward some possible future. Shaonan's point: people only get anxious when they have choices; when they don't, they just work. You don't get anxious when a grizzly bear is chasing you. Existential crisis and crisis of existence don't happen at the same time. Right now, what concerns him most is his children's growth, how to be an agent that cares for people rather than efficiency, and understanding himself.

1:11:15 Ask why you'd bet, not what you should learn in the AI age
The conversation closes on a more fundamental question: rather than asking what you should learn in the age of AI, the better question is what you actually want to commit to, what you're willing to invest time and attention in over the long term. As tools can do more and more, if you don't know what you want to use them for, each new possibility becomes a burden of ‘should learn this’—and in the end it's just exhausting. Possibilities may be infinite, but the time you can invest is always finite.

item.title: Salesforce's M&A Chief: Great Technology Dies Without Distribution
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-a16z-salesforce并购负责人-好技术没有分销渠道-照样会被饿死/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-a16z-salesforce并购负责人-好技术没有分销渠道-照样会被饿死/
item.description: John Somorjai says software can be built faster and cheaper than ever, but startups still need years and constant equity dilution to build sales networks reaching all customers—which is precisely why M&A creates value for both Salesforce and its acquisition targets.
item.content:encoded:
John Somorjai says software can be built faster and cheaper than ever, but startups still need years and constant equity dilution to build sales networks reaching all customers—which is precisely why M&A creates value for both Salesforce and its acquisition targets.

Rare public disclosure of Salesforce's billion-dollar M&A machine's internal scoring framework, due diligence red flags, and judgment on first-market valuation bubbles—practical reference for founders considering acquisition or fundraising.

8:14 Test an acquisition internally before committing to purchase
Salesforce piloted FIN on help.salesforce.com and deployed it in just 14 days. Today FIN handles over 40% of website traffic, resolving 65% of queries without human handoff. For Somorjai, this speed from deployment to impact is the core metric for acquisition decisions—the faster value emerges, the better the acquisition.

10:15 A built sales force is the ultimate acquisition trigger
Salesforce's 15,000 sales representatives are the moat that forces acquisition. Once a product is integrated into this channel, a small team can instantly reach all customer segments globally. Building distribution yourself takes years and constant equity dilution. This is why acquisition creates value for both Salesforce and its targets.

17:38 Acquisitions take six to nine months from start to finish
Software development has never been faster or cheaper, making the build-versus-buy decision harder to judge. Teams evaluate product roadmap, internal talent gaps (especially AI engineers, who are extremely hard to hire), and whether internal build speed can keep pace. But Somorjai notes that acquisition itself takes six to nine months from initial contact to full integration. The real question: can you build faster than that?

22:51 The Slack thesis only got stronger with AI agents
When Salesforce acquired Slack in 2020, the thesis was that Slack represented the interface for humans collaborating with applications. No one anticipated the AI agent era. But Somorjai says the original logic remains sound and is now validated beyond expectations, because Slack has become the ideal conversational interface for AI agents. Five years on, Slack revenue has nearly tripled and is Salesforce's fastest-growing product.

29:05 Track the future: Salesforce Ventures shifted to AI and robots
Salesforce Ventures started in 2009 backing ecosystem partners like DocuSign and Twilio, then expanded to industry-defining companies like Snowflake and Wiz. In early 2023, it established a $1 billion AI fund and invested in Anthropic, Mistral, Cohere, 11 Labs, and Runway. Now it's moving into physical AI and robotics. The underlying logic never changed: find companies that will create enterprise value in the future, whether or not they're core to today's business.

35:21 No new CRM company will ever beat Salesforce
Facing a wave of AI-native CRM startups, Somorjai is direct: existing CRM technology is already good enough, and Salesforce keeps improving it. He has not seen any new CRM differentiated enough to grow into a multi-billion-dollar company. When pressed on a possible SMB market opportunity, he concedes it might exist but dismisses it as too small for venture capital scale.

37:27 Valuations above $100 billion have almost no buyers
Somorjai is blunt about the first market: irresponsible behavior is rampant and valuations are widely inflated. Real exit paths are narrow—fewer than 1% of companies go public. Once a valuation exceeds $100 billion, the pool of potential acquirers shrinks sharply. This valuation-to-reality gap will eventually clear. Many companies simply cannot grow to match their valuations. Yet he also notes that each year he sees many dying companies trying to sell—a dynamic the press doesn't report.

42:48 ARR hides churn, and security can kill a deal
In due diligence, Somorjai's biggest warning sign from founders is fixating on ARR—it masks true customer churn. Security is a separate, hard constraint. Among 14 due diligence functions, only the security team has unilateral veto power over a deal. He cites one case where penetration testing not only exposed full source code access but also granted attackers entry to the CEO's laptop and employee data—damage too severe to remedy, and the deal died. Most security gaps can be fixed via covenants or pre-closing remediation.

item.title: Voters overwhelmingly reject data centers, but big tech will likely still win
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-sharptech-选民几乎全票否决数据中心-但赢家大概率还是大厂/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-sharptech-选民几乎全票否决数据中心-但赢家大概率还是大厂/
item.description: 43 of 44 local referendums against data centers passed; even mayors and lawmakers were recalled. Yet capital, credit, and land advantages remain concentrated in Amazon and Google—the scarcer compute becomes, the better their position.
item.content:encoded:
43 of 44 local referendums against data centers passed; even mayors and lawmakers were recalled. Yet capital, credit, and land advantages remain concentrated in Amazon and Google—the scarcer compute becomes, the better their position.

Three threads interweave: the data center backlash, Google's earnings collapse, and SpaceX's space data center plans. The analysis in the middle—on big tech's financing advantages and space-based compute—is where the insight concentrates; don't stop at the political opening.

4:13 Even Texas, data centers' last refuge, is now blocking expansion
Texas was long viewed as data centers' last refuge: independent power grid, abundant natural gas, friendly policy environment. But the newly elected governor promised to pause new approvals until the state legislature reviews—and Texas's legislature meets only every two years. This could mean an indefinite halt. More alarming for incumbents: mayors and officials who backed data centers were recalled. Officials now fear losing their seats even without formal referendums, making them politically cautious regardless of policy.

7:46 The opposition isn't about facts; it's emotional and ideological
The root objection isn't factual. Like the ‘fake news’ phenomenon, voters don't believe false claims first and then oppose data centers; they harbor resentment toward tech elites first, then hunt for justifications. If one anti-data-center argument is debunked, they simply pivot to another—because what they really oppose is the entire AI-painted future being imposed on them.

9:19 Only people who love advertising will buy into AI's promises
The AI industry will only convince those already conditioned by advertising. Good advertising first convinces you that you have a need, then offers the solution; AI just asserts it replaces workers. Deeper problem: the industry treats human desires as completely modelable and substitutable variables—a planned-economy logic, not an understanding that humans perpetually generate new needs.

20:51 Data centers promise long-term gains, but big tech skips the short-term bills
Loudoun County exemplifies the data center virtuous cycle: local property taxes down, electricity down over a thirty-year arc. But the catch: data centers drive up local electricity costs and stress the grid in their early years. Big tech doesn't subsidize this transition—it demands communities subsidize them instead. For the industry's long-term story to be credible, it must first absorb the short- and medium-term pain it inflicts.

36:27 Sunk launch costs make space data centers suddenly rational
SpaceX's orbital data center concept mirrors shipping's marginal-cost logic: ship depreciation is sunk; if fuel and port fees are covered, sailing even at accounting loss makes sense. SpaceX has already built launch infrastructure for Starlink. Once that capital is treated as ‘already spent, not to be recalculated,’ sending server racks to orbit only requires covering marginal costs—suddenly the calculation shifts from absurd to plausible.

44:49 Compute scarcity turns big tech's existing advantages into overwhelming dominance
In a compute-constrained world—where politics and grid capacity become limiting factors—incumbents dominate. Amazon and Google hold land, power, permits, and community relationships, enabling expansion without starting from zero. Their cash flows are thicker, credit ratings higher, borrowing costs lower. When raising equity, they have real profitable businesses backing the bet. By contrast, all the equity value of Anthropic and OpenAI rests on a single outcome: whether their models succeed.

1:01:23 Google's pitch now echoes Meta's old playbook on scaling then monetizing
Google's latest earnings language mirrors Meta's old pitch on Stories and Reels: first perfect the product, scale it globally, then layer in advertising. Google Search's ads still live in traditional results pages; the AI mode carries almost no advertisements yet. But users query more frequently and spend longer in AI mode. Google's wager: once ads migrate into AI search, it becomes the new cash machine, as Reels did from initial drag to current engine.

1:21:41 The internet economy is shifting from mass scale toward intimate groups
AI makes building individual software easier, but because everyone can build, single vibe-coding apps lack scalable monetization. The real economic value flows to custom-built software for tight-knit groups. The hardest-hit businesses are those built on Google traffic for mass reach—Reddit recognized this shift and abandoned the pageview chase, pivoting instead to maximizing revenue per logged-in user. The internet economy is migrating from mass-scale reach to high-engagement small circles.

item.title: Gen Z's digital literacy has fallen behind millennials' despite universal school laptops
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-raisinggh-人手一台校发电脑后-z世代数字素养反而不如千禧一代/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-raisinggh-人手一台校发电脑后-z世代数字素养反而不如千禧一代/
item.description: Introduce a tool before mastering the underlying skill and you guarantee the skill won't be learned—precisely what happened when 88% of American students received school laptops.
item.content:encoded:
Introduce a tool before mastering the underlying skill and you guarantee the skill won't be learned—precisely what happened when 88% of American students received school laptops.

This episode demonstrates the principle 'tools before skill' through calculators, AI, SAT reform and international data, giving parents and teachers a working framework for deciding when to introduce technology.

7:17 Teaching the skill must come before introducing the tool
This principle emerged from the 1980s calculator debate: when should children use calculators? Answer: 'when you no longer need one'—once students understand arithmetic, a calculator is an aid; introduce it before they do and it permanently blocks skill formation. Children learn only to operate the machine until someone approves. This is what's happening at scale in schools distributing laptops today.

10:18 Teachers mid-career confuse engagement with learning
Those most confident in technology aren't veteran educators (20+ years, who've seen before-and-after and mostly reject it) or newcomers (who prioritize relationship-building). They're mid-career teachers—5 to 15 years in—trained by technology themselves. They judge tech 'effective' because students stay engaged. But engagement and learning are different metrics: swiping TikTok keeps you engaged without teaching you anything.

24:50 Learning happens through biological synchrony between teacher and student
Horvath redefines empathy not as emotion or personality but as a 'transpersonal emergent property': when two people synchronise, their heart rates and breathing align, their brain images converge. In sync with a teacher, students don't listen passively—they think alongside the teacher. Comprehension and motivation spike. Screens have no biology; they can never synchronise and actively sever the empathy already flowing between people.

36:04 Technology amplifies rather than closes the equity gap
Neil Postman's 1995 air-conditioning metaphor holds: tools never bridge equity gaps; they enlarge them. Horvath ran a counterfactual on New York data—assume minority students use tech all day and white students never use it—and the equity gap didn't shrink; it expanded 26%. The variable that works is 'every student has a teacher who genuinely cares.' Tech can't solve that.

39:10 Growing up with tools actually undermines digital literacy
Horvath often asks at AI education forums: 'How old are you and who taught you to use AI?' The answer is typically 30-something—a generation that never took a class on it yet outperforms kids who grew up onscreen. Tests show Gen Z and Alpha score high only on 'operating tools,' falling behind across every dimension that defines real literacy: creative use, critical use, safe communication. Those abilities depend on knowledge you bring to the tool, not what the tool teaches.

44:22 When SAT embedded powerful calculators, students learned to trick them
Until 2013, only four of America's top 50 universities allowed calculators at the college level—schools insisted students master arithmetic first. Last year, SAT eliminated its no-calculator math section entirely, embedding a calculator so powerful it can 'crack' every problem. Now tutoring doesn't teach math; it teaches kids how to coax the machine into solving it for them.

50:34 Test scores rose because the tests themselves were quietly redefined
NAEP and tests that maintain their measures show reading at historic lows, math barely back to 1992 levels. Even working memory—'remember seven digits'—supposedly a fixed constant, has fallen from seven to 5.5. But SAT scores rose after last year's redesign because reading was redefined as skimming 75-word excerpts (one question per 54 words) and writing redefined as spotting spelling errors. Rename the test and scores improve.

58:57 Countries that rejected EdTech longest are now seeing the steepest declines
China, Japan, South Korea and Singapore were the globe's lightest users of education technology before COVID—despite digital-dependent economies, they'd never scaled tech into classrooms. The pandemic forced adoption. Since then, even Singapore, whose test scores only ever climbed, has seen performance fall noticeably.

item.title: Anthropic's Q3 slowdown was compute-constrained, not demand-constrained
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-complexsys-anthropic三季度放缓不是需求退潮-是算力不够卖/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-complexsys-anthropic三季度放缓不是需求退潮-是算力不够卖/
item.description: The S-1 reveals Q3 had to fill half its compute purchases with a $500M high-cost spot market—long-term capacity was fully booked, not because customer demand for tokens dried up.
item.content:encoded:
The S-1 reveals Q3 had to fill half its compute purchases with a $500M high-cost spot market—long-term capacity was fully booked, not because customer demand for tokens dried up.

Beyond valuation noise, this episode mines S-1 details for real signals—matched-giving expenses, governance structures, and default mechanics on compute commitments—angles financial media seldom covers.

1:35 Existential risks in passive voice: hedging for both audiences
Zvi notes that Anthropic's S-1 discussion of existential risk uses only passive voice and glosses over it—attempting to tell two incompatible stories at once: ‘we're a highly profitable compute supercomputer company’ to investors, while elsewhere claiming ‘what we built could kill everyone.’ Lawyers instinctively minimize disclosure since S-1 filings become evidence in future litigation. But Zvi argues the silence is itself revealing: if you genuinely believed your stated existential risks, choosing to stay quiet in the document where you should be most transparent says something about who you actually are.

8:26 Three founders can maintain company control indefinitely if they stay
Anthropic created a Class F shareholder class pooling founder votes with 50.1% voting control on broad corporate matters. The company has roughly seven formal founders, but this super-voting block persists as long as just three remain employed—sufficient, by Zvi's estimate, to outlast ‘the point when the dust settles on the world's fate.’ The company also chartered a long-term giving trust nominally controlling four board seats: the board selects three, the trust selects three, and a seventh seat requires founder approval or else goes to Class E shareholders (employees who've donated stock to charity), who are assumed to align with the founders.

11:33 Uncapped 3:1 giving match may be capitalism's costliest employee perk
The founders committed to donating 80% of their personal shares to charity, coupled with an employee giving-match program offering 3:1 matching without limit—unprecedented in capitalism's history. Standard companies offer 1:1 matching capped at a few thousand dollars. Anthropic employees can donate $20M to charity and trigger a $60M company match. With thousands of employees holding nine-figure equity stakes, this may become one of capitalism's single most expensive unilateral decisions. The Q3 non-cash charge of ~$24B in unattributed equity compensation hints at what's coming, and Zvi expects it won't be the last.

22:25 Q3's slowdown was compute-constrained, not demand-constrained
Analysts widely interpreted Anthropic's Q3 revenue slowdown as evidence demand has plateaued. Patrick's retrospective reading is opposite: the S-1 makes plain the company faces chronic compute constraints, with procurement requiring 12–18 months lead time—meaning they had to commit in early 2025 to compute volumes for models not yet released. The smoking gun: they spent $5B on spot-market compute that quarter, representing fully half their compute spending, well above normal—signaling long-term capacity was fully booked and customer token demand remained queued.

31:56 $141B raised, ~$10B burned, yet carrying ~$800B in compute commitments
Anthropic raised $141B cumulatively and retains $131B in cash and investments; actual cash consumption totals roughly $10B. Hundreds of billions in reported losses stem mainly from mark-to-market losses on convertible debt as stock price climbed—Zvi frames this as pure accounting convention, not real cash hemorrhage. The material number is the ~$800B in forward compute commitments on the balance sheet—effectively spreading years of massive future spending across current-quarter reports, structurally similar to a massive real-estate lease obligation.

46:49 Wall Street and tech circles price the same company on completely different books
Wall Street values Anthropic as ‘a very impressive software company.’ Tech insiders want to shake Wall Street awake and say: Google's entire commercial history might be merely this business's bootloader. Google would exhaust its entire free cash flow, max out its credit lines, just to own this franchise—not just to defend search from disintermediation, but because this business exceeds every business in capitalist history. Investment banks haven't yet priced that thesis into their DCF models. Zvi thinks that omission is precisely where a credible bear case finds its foundation.

59:44 No one taught it Japanese—the model figured it out on its own
Patrick witnessed a research lab demo an unreleased model that had explicitly not been trained on Japanese, with zero in-house Japanese training data involved. Yet the researchers suspected the model had reverse-engineered Japanese grammar and structure from raw English-language internet content alone. Patrick tested it on a CNN news segment the training data couldn't have seen, and—as someone with 20 years' experience as a professional translator—said the model's Japanese might surpass his own. This exemplifies the Bitter Lesson: scale up the model and unexpected capabilities emerge that nobody trained it to have.

1:12:02 Binance lost $5B to hackers; the industry's security debt runs $500B
Hours before recording, North Korean hackers breached Binance for over $5B. Patrick argues that the AI-enabled hacking wave won't primarily wield research-lab models themselves, but rather open-source weights distilled from those labs. He estimates the industry's total security technical debt at roughly $500B (priced at pre-AI rates), a sum payable only by betting everything on AI-powered defense. Zvi's outlook is darker: this isn't a one-time invoice because any operator can now parallelize attack probes; vulnerability discovery will compound.

item.content:encoded:
As VCs crowd into passive shareholding in consensus picks like Databricks and Anthropic, Naimi warns: history shows almost no strategy that everyone finds simple sustains long-term outperformance.

No macro-commentary boilerplate—all first-hand details on pricing mechanics, fund-raising cadence, and infrastructure-finance tools from primary market operations.

2:09 Second-tier allocations in the same round now cost 3 to 5 times as much
VCs that miss the main allocation get a second tier in the same round, priced 3–5x the main. Silicon Valley calls this the "cuck tranche." Naimi reframes it not as market failure but as these companies being capital-intensive enough that founders won't close in one draw. Most VC shops have been frozen out of one or two allocation tiers at least once.

10:29 Mega-funds deploy 2 to 3 times faster than their budgets assume
VCs size funds on 18–24 months of planned deployment, but mega-platform funds have actually deployed in 12–18 months—two to three times faster than projected. This forces a binary choice: maintain position size but write far fewer checks, or write the same number of checks and accept dilution. The first tests stock-picking skill; the second bets that diversification hedges not being a top-tier picker.

12:35 Liquidity for most LPs depends on success in just four companies
Some LPs put 35–50% of assets into private equity. Drill down and 30–50% of that sits in just four names: SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks. Real LP cash doesn't flow from sector health—it flows from exposure to these four. LPs without these bets are drawing almost no liquidity this cycle.

15:43 Burning billions to reach 85% margin demands new finance tools
Anthropic's S-1 revealed $140 billion cumulative fundraising, $10 billion burned, $132 billion on the balance sheet, and 85% gross margin. Extreme burn married to high margin forces innovation: General Catalyst's customer-value fund, lending on "every $10M deployed unlocks $30M revenue," has proven viable. But the industry still needs purpose-built infrastructure finance instead of pure equity.

21:53 Nearly 100 model labs burn annual compute budgets in single training runs
The NeoLab landscape exploded from two or three players to 80–90 companies at $1–5 billion valuations. Naimi's example: one firm is raising a second $1 billion for a single training run next year, then expects another $5 billion the year after. Real constraint isn't equity—it's securing 5–10x leverage as non-dilutive debt at rational terms. Recent stress in public infrastructure debt has spiked that cost.

24:01 Endpoint assumptions jumped from $100 billion to $1 trillion; seed valuations followed
In 2016, best-case endpoint was $10 billion. By 2021, Stripe and Databricks pushed it to $100 billion. Now SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI have proven $1 trillion is real, so every early company gets priced as if it can reach $1 trillion—even entering at $100 million.

26:05 Backing unfashionable bets early separates top 5 percent from top 25 percent
Passive plays on hot sectors top out around 25th percentile. Top 5% requires early conviction in neglected bets. Example: Conduit, a brain-computer interface company. Nine months ago, BCI was ignored. The team built a headset reading neural activity at 80% accuracy. Eight to ten weeks later, BCI went hot—Conduit's round drew 13 term sheets and massively oversubscribed. Smarter investors see the wave before the crowd.

33:18 Crowding into "safe" mega-rounds is itself the largest risk signal
When early markets are chaotic, one hedge is mega-sized positions in proven winners. Stripe, valued at $100 billion in 2021, is now worth $179 billion, yielding 11–12% annualized over five years—still placing in the top 25% for VC returns. But over the past 18 months, VCs have embraced this same playbook: huge checks into a handful of known bets, stay passive. History shows almost no strategy that everyone finds simple sustains long-term market outperformance.

item.content:encoded:
From Texas to Virginia, governors of data center-building states have uniformly shifted to the Democratic Party—the tax incentives and zero-regulation environment once taken for granted are being renegotiated.

Political gossip and genuine hard-core macroeconomics woven together: how the Senate's structural advantage determines Federal Reserve appointments, AI spending approaching 8% of GDP, and shifting capital-expenditure financing structures. Information-dense throughout.

1:03 Polls got the Senate right; Wall Street got the stock market wrong
Nate Silver had insisted the Senate was not simply a coin flip, and Democrats secured it with a far larger margin than expected. Meanwhile, Bank of America strategist Hartnett warned a Democratic victory would tank the S&P 500 by 10%—yet the index rose about 1.5% after results came in, exposing the market's default assumption ‘Democratic victory is bearish for stocks’as unfounded. Only red-state-linked individual stocks were hammered the day after.

4:06 The Senate's real leverage is the Supreme Court and the Federal Reserve
Senate seats track state count, not population—Kansas and Iowa each get two seats just like New York, cementing Republicans' structural advantage. That advantage determines not only legislation but who sits on the Supreme Court and Federal Reserve board. Skanda noted this blue tsunami may not be repeatable, but it proves Democrats have multiple paths to secure 50 to 51 votes, reshaping personnel appointments for years forward.

9:14 Texas swung from purple to deep blue overnight
Texas political circles had long harbored the fantasy that the state would turn purple—once dismissed as naive. This election flipped not just the governorship but all downstream offices: state comptroller, lieutenant governor, state board of education, University of Texas regents. It's been described as a ‘neutron bomb’strike—the building remains standing but everyone inside was replaced. Texas's business court, erected to retain corporations by modeling Delaware's laws, suddenly seems less politically stable than the business community assumed.

12:17 Data center powerhouse states all elected Democratic governors
Texas, Georgia, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia, even Wisconsin—states that tech companies have treated as prime data center destinations—all now have Democratic governors. Data center power-approval authority sits mainly at state and local levels, not federal. The shift is already flowing into corporate practice: under public pressure, OpenAI announced changes to its data center model, dropping nondisclosure agreements and no longer billing residents for electricity—evidence that political headwinds penetrate commercial terms faster than expected.

17:37 Capital spending is shifting from accounting abstraction to real financial pressure
Historically, major cloud providers financed data center capex mostly with retained cash, recorded as depreciation on the balance sheet and never hitting EBITDA. But the financing structure is now visibly changing: companies are borrowing in the debt markets, and Oracle is issuing new equity to fund capital investment. This marks capex's shift from a line item easily overlooked to a genuine squeeze on cash flow and the balance sheet, with markets now rewarding capital efficiency instead of merely rewarding spending scale.

19:40 Powell will serve until 2028; his successor faces confirmation obstacles
Powell's term runs through early 2028 and he will very likely complete it, provided the Federal Reserve itself avoids scrutiny. But even if an opening emerges, the nomination-and-confirmation process before his term ends will be hard to finish, because any successor must clear the Senate now controlled by Democrats. Many of these senators are in six-year terms after flipping unexpected seats in once-red states like South Carolina and Mississippi—a potential one-time gain in the near term, but one with real and durable impact on personnel appointments for years to come.

27:49 AI-related spending now approaches 8% of GDP; the economic cycle follows it
Sum together tech hardware, software, and industrial equipment directly tied to AI: the aggregate is already approaching 8% of US GDP—large enough to drive the entire economic cycle. Skanda argues the non-AI economy has actually been solid these past six months, just less flashy than the AI side. But if AI capex truly cools, the transition will likely not be gradual—it could flip like a switch and stop nearly cold. Traditional sectors such as real estate that might step in remain depressed and unlikely to quickly absorb the overflow.

33:56 The political map was redrawn overnight; Watergate offers the only real parallel
Some draw a line between this election and the Democratic surge after Watergate—not because of scale but because two conditions converged: high inflation and an unpopular president. Yet Tracy cautions that when 2024 ended, everyone believed the Trump-led Republican coalition was now permanently locked in, even hitting record support among minorities—and in less than a year the whole picture inverted. That suggests today's consensus about the two-party map may prove just as fragile as the consensus from two years ago.

item.title: Milk cartons scared a generation of Americans, yet never found a single child
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-cautionary-牛奶盒寻人运动吓坏一代美国人-却没找回一个孩子/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-cautionary-牛奶盒寻人运动吓坏一代美国人-却没找回一个孩子/
item.description: Missing children's photos on milk cartons made a generation guard against stranger abduction, but tracing through the program, they never actually helped find a child—only obscured poverty and domestic violence, the more common dangers children face.
item.content:encoded:
Missing children's photos on milk cartons made a generation guard against stranger abduction, but tracing through the program, they never actually helped find a child—only obscured poverty and domestic violence, the more common dangers children face.

Three American historical objects form a single theme: how simplified symbols—a safe, milk cartons, a time clock—quietly displace complex problems that deserve serious attention; medium-to-high information density.

9:38 The first time imagining centuries ahead, humans didn't know what mattered
The Century Safe was sealed in 1876 and scheduled to open in 1976, but its planners confused importance with curiosity—inside were public symbols like congressional photos, prohibition pamphlets, and paid signatures, nothing that mattered. Historian Jill Lepore said nothing in the box was useful. Roman Mars noted this was humanity's first serious attempt to imagine its traces surviving a century, yet it traded what truly held value—personal records now so scarce that an archived email may be worth more than most published works—for what looked like big history.

16:58 The ‘dangerous stranger’ label masks more common threats to children
The milk carton campaign began with two boys' disappearances; dairies printed photos on packaging, using milk's daily purchase and updateable images to spread the word. Cases were classified as dangerous stranger abduction, a frame that fixed public attention on strangers. But the actual harms children face—poverty, alcoholic households, abuse by people close to them—occur dozens to hundreds of times more often, yet were systematically ignored because they lack drama.

19:00 Halloween poisoned candy never happened but became perfect cover
There is no documented case of a stranger poisoning Halloween candy; the real Halloween danger is children being hit by cars after dark. The one ‘poisoned candy death’ was a father who poisoned his own son for insurance money—he felt safe doing it because the public assumed strangers poison candy, so no one would suspect him. It's the episode's sharpest point: a false threat, repeatedly amplified, ends up sheltering the people actually doing harm.

22:06 The milk carton campaign terrified a generation but found zero children
The campaign was brief but frightened Mars's entire generation. Yet traced back, not a single child was found because of a milk carton. The only related case came from a random traffic stop. It didn't change outcomes—it changed the order of fears in people's minds. Strangers' faces became fear number one, while poverty and family violence were pushed behind.

27:12 The time clock was built to defend workers, then sold to their bosses
Willard Bundy was an engineer fascinated by clock mechanics who invented the first time clock so workers could prove their hours hadn't been stolen. That version didn't sell. His brother Harold flipped the pitch: don't tell workers it protects them, tell factory owners workers are lazy, stealing time—buy this clock to manage them. A tool's meaning depends on who buys it first, not the inventor's intent.

30:17 Taylorism flattened workers into a boiler and a pump
Frederick Taylor timed every movement on the factory floor with a stopwatch: handling a tool counted as pause time, speaking counted as pause time. He forced out the theoretical minimum, then demanded workers maintain it all day. A factory owner of the era described workers as "movable power plants"—the stomach is a boiler, the heart a pump. The description is accurate, but it strips out what actually matters: belonging, will, trust.

31:17 Even Lenin couldn't resist copying Taylorism's blueprint
Before the revolution, Lenin condemned Taylorism as a terrible, oppressive tool of capitalist class war. After the revolution succeeded, when the Soviets had to actually manage factories, he introduced Taylorism. The reversal exposes its true nature: not a capitalism-specific disease, but something any power structure wanting to reduce complex humans to an efficiency number inevitably reaches for.

32:21 Screenshot every five minutes: Taylorism's digital-age upgrade
Remote monitoring software auto-screenshots every few minutes and tracks activity. Harford mentions an earlier episode about a female manager whose system photographed her screen every 5 minutes. Real work went unmeasured: bathroom breaks, walks to think, pen and paper, mentoring someone on a call. Taylorism faded because happiness and trust were hard to measure. Now managers believe they have enough data—and they're making the same mistake with better tools.

item.title: The number Anthropic's filing dodges sets the IPO valuation ceiling
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-latetalk-anthropic招股书没敢给的数字-决定了ipo估值天花板/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-latetalk-anthropic招股书没敢给的数字-决定了ipo估值天花板/
item.description: The filing sidestepped the one critical figure—October revenue. Whether the $1.5 trillion valuation holds depends entirely on whether that number can support the year-end extrapolation to $1 trillion annualized revenue.
item.content:encoded:
The filing sidestepped the one critical figure—October revenue. Whether the $1.5 trillion valuation holds depends entirely on whether that number can support the year-end extrapolation to $1 trillion annualized revenue.

A fund manager who has long traded both long and short in AI compute stocks dissects the filing's accounting techniques and contract terms point by point. For those seeking valuation logic, not gossip.

4:01 Customer concentration improves, but cash flow conceals the catch
Rob's biggest surprise in the filing was positive: Q3 shows the top five customers account for only ~20% of revenue, with the single largest under 10%—proof Anthropic isn't dependent on a handful of megadeals. But the same document hides a problem. Their ~$1.5 trillion CPU rental agreement with Broadcom is classified as an operating lease, not a finance lease. This accounting move strips that cash outflow from the operating cash flow line entirely, artificially inflating the ‘positive free cash flow’ claim. Account for it correctly, and the actual cash position is worse than disclosed.

13:14 Growth plummets from 144% to 45%—fine for company, not for market
Q2 revenue was $115.55 billion with a 144% quarter-over-quarter jump. Q3 hit $168 billion, but growth collapsed to 45% QoQ. The company considers 45% fine operationally. The market, though, had been linearly extrapolating outward, expecting ~$1 trillion annualized revenue by year-end. At Q3's rate of growth, year-end ARR would likely land only in the $850–950 billion range—far short of the prior bullish consensus. That gap is why the market took the stock down before October even arrived.

20:16 Valuation above $1.5 trillion hinges entirely on October numbers
Initial expectations had IPO valuation at $2 trillion. By mid-October, some investors were circulating a downward revision to $1.5 trillion. To defend the $1.5 trillion mark, the company needs October data that can be extrapolated to ~$1 trillion year-end ARR. If October lands where Q3's extrapolation suggests—$850–950 billion—or lower still, the final price will likely be well below $1.5 trillion. Rob estimates it could drop into the $1.2–1.3 trillion range instead.

26:18 Cloud providers take 37%—higher than Apple's tax, but worth it
The cloud provider take-rate works out to roughly 37%, higher than Apple's App Store cut of 30%. Importantly, this goes into R&D expense rather than hitting revenue as a direct reduction. Rob argues it's worth the premium: Anthropic's sales team is tiny and can't yet serve every enterprise customer directly. Cloud providers bring three values at once—the compute capacity itself, customer relationships (enterprises trust vendors they already work with), and capital (Amazon invested directly). The combination justifies the 37% rate at this stage.

37:20 Over $600 billion in compute contracts, but less than half are actually binding
Anthropic's disclosed long-term compute contracts add up to more than $600 billion. But the headline number obscures a crucial detail: not all of it is actually locked in. The SpaceX AI deal tops out at $1.205 trillion but remains non-cancellable only through early 2027; after that either side can exit with 90 days' notice. Nscale's $446 billion agreement can be walked away from entirely. Only the Broadcom contract—roughly $1.612 trillion—is mutual non-cancellable, and Anthropic must post guarantees and equipment collateral. The truly rigid, irreversible contracts total around $3 trillion, not $600 billion.

41:21 WeWork's trap: long-term cost lock, short-term revenue risk
Anthropic's longest compute contracts run 20 years, exposing the company to inflation in electricity and infrastructure costs over the entire life. Yet with many large customers, there's no matching long-term revenue commitment. Rob compares this to WeWork's broken model: cost side is a long-term lease (multi-year, non-cancellable), revenue side is a short-term lease (customers can leave anytime). If downstream demand weakens, revenue cash evaporates quickly while the long-term compute bills keep arriving. Money flowing out exceeds money flowing in.

44:24 Coding's gains are exhausted; the frontier is replacing knowledge workers
The coding vertical is already highly penetrated and fundamentally limited—roughly 1 million developers worldwide is the addressable pool. The real prize is replacing knowledge work. Anthropic's own measurement pegs the global payroll for knowledge workers at $40 trillion. Both Anthropic and OpenAI are now paying data-labeling firms like Mercor and Scale AI to recruit finance professionals, lawyers, doctors, and other domain experts to describe their actual workflows in detail. Those proprietary datasets are being used to train models, laying the groundwork for displacing white-collar work at scale.

53:28 To spot a bubble, ignore supply—watch how steep the demand curve is
To judge whether AI is in a bubble, the key is not supply-side factors like memory or chip oversupply. It's the steepness of the demand curve. The capex trajectory is fairly locked in and predictable. What's uncertain is how fast revenue demand can rise to meet it. That gap determines how many more years the industry can sustain burning capital before the two curves intersect. Rob sees current market panic as an overreaction to recent slowness. That said, no one can be certain that giants like Amazon's confidence in future growth will actually pan out.

item.content:encoded:
Banks and pharmaceutical companies have raised AI budgets to their highest-ever priority, but Zhang Lu believes enterprises must traverse two stages—automation and optimization—to truly transform workflows, making year-one explosive growth like coding impossible.

Zhang Lu maintains long-standing access to Silicon Valley Fortune 500 CIO and CTO networks, offering on-the-ground insights into corporate AI budgets, deployment velocity, and startup opportunities beyond the prospectus figures—essential listening for B2B practitioners and investors.

4:02 Embedded in workflows, Claude has become enterprise infrastructure
Zhang Lu says the prospectus figure that struck her most wasn't revenue growth but customer composition: roughly 11,000 to 12,000 enterprise customers spending over $100,000 annually, with about 2,000 spending over $1 million yearly. This reveals Claude isn't merely a trial tool but deeply embedded in workflows—functioning like infrastructure. The result: far faster upsell velocity and opportunity.

10:03 Enterprises cut closed-source adoption from 57 to 14 percent in six months
A report from two weeks prior showed large enterprises' adoption of cutting-edge, closed-source models collapsed from 57% to 14% in half a year, shifting toward open-source deployment. AT&T publicly committed 60-70% of internal AI budgets to open-source; Nvidia's Jensen Huang also publicly backs the open-source ecosystem. But Zhang Lu doesn't expect this to squeeze Anthropic and OpenAI from the market—AI is permeating the entire economy, expanding the pie itself. They'll simply have more competitors dividing it.

20:09 FTX collapse forced liquidation of SBF's Anthropic stake for debt
Anthropic's early financing was rocky. In May 2023, Spark Capital made a non-consensus bet at Anthropic's ~$4.5 billion valuation when markets weren't sure whether they could support a second frontier model company. More dramatically: FTX founder SBF had invested in Anthropic too, but after FTX's bankruptcy, his shares were largely auctioned off for debt repayment. Zhang Lu noted that had FTX not collapsed, those investment returns could have covered much of what SBF needed to pay back.

35:15 US bank's 2026 AI budget exceeds 100 billion dollars annually
Zhang Lu disclosed that a major US bank's Chief AI Officer told her the bank's AI budget this year has already reached over 100 billion dollars—shocking even her. She observes a pattern: once one company in an industry commits heavily to AI, the rest race to catch up fast. Companies fear falling behind AI-savvy competitors more than being disrupted by startups.

36:44 Enterprise AI transformation requires automation first, then optimization—years not quarters
Zhang Lu divides enterprise AI into two stages: Business Automation (embedding AI in existing workflows for cost cuts and efficiency gains), then Business Optimization (lifting revenues, showing in financial statements). Most enterprises don't want to scrap systems and rebuild; they want agents to keep working with their current software. She estimates stage one alone taking 3-5 years to roll out broadly, with stage two taking longer. Don't expect AI to transform the entire economy in one or two years.

38:15 A 500 million monthly bill taught enterprises to ration AI use
Zhang Lu relayed that a consulting firm heard an unnamed large enterprise's single-month Claude bill suddenly spike to nearly 500 million dollars, shocking their CFO. This unsustainable burn quickly triggered cost controls: major tech companies shifted from early encouragement to burn tokens to now strictly rationing usage. This partly explains why enterprises favor open-source models—closed-source pricing is prohibitive.

56:27 Pharma's real bottleneck is raising clinical success rates, not discovering targets
Regarding Anthropic and OpenAI's bet on AI for Science (drug discovery, mathematical proofs), Zhang Lu thinks near-term revenue contribution is unlikely, though reasoning ability will improve. She pushes back on AI pharma narratives: even if AI expands target discovery from 2-3 targets to hundreds, those don't directly become drugs—clinical trials consume the cash. She's bullish on using AI to identify, from hundreds of targets, the few with highest clinical success rates, lifting success above 50-60%—that's genuinely valuable to the industry.

1:08:33 Physical AI failures mean deaths, not hallucinations—regulation must come first
Zhang Lu recently spent considerable time thinking about AI regulation—her UN AI for Good board just held a 2+ hour session on it. Language model hallucinations were once funny; Physical AI failures risk human lives and catastrophic accidents. CTOs she meets are anxious, insisting that regulation and technical safeguards must be embedded before scaling physical AI—a prerequisite no high-regulation industry like healthcare can bypass.

item.title: AI can synthesize viruses; what's missing is robots with dexterous hands
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-05-cogrev-病毒合成能力已不缺ai-缺的是机器人的灵巧双手/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-05-cogrev-病毒合成能力已不缺ai-缺的是机器人的灵巧双手/
item.description: Monrad believes model intelligence is nearly sufficient, but turning designs into live viruses still requires precise wet lab work—which depends on robots with dexterous hands, and current robots aren't dexterous enough.
item.content:encoded:
Monrad believes model intelligence is nearly sufficient, but turning designs into live viruses still requires precise wet lab work—which depends on robots with dexterous hands, and current robots aren't dexterous enough.

If you care where the real bottleneck between AI and biosecurity lies, this episode provides specific numbers and mechanisms, not generic risk talk.

9:09 The final bottleneck is robots, not artificial intelligence
Monrad divides biosecurity risk into four stages: historical biological weapons, AI enhancing human capability (which he believes is now underway), AI coercing humans (using model-based deception or coercion to make humans complete physical tasks—he views emerging social engineering waves in other domains as leading indicators), and fully autonomous end-to-end scenarios with no human involvement. On the last category, his judgment is specific: models will soon be "smart enough," but there are simply "no thumbs dexterous enough." He frames this not as an intelligence problem but a robotics problem—though he acknowledges the situation will change by the 2030s.

25:29 Hundreds of thousands of people can today reconstruct transmissible influenza
Genome length is a rough proxy for difficulty: smallpox is about 186,000 base pairs, polio about 9,000, Ebola about 20,000 to 30,000. Activating assembled genomes into live viruses presents another hurdle. But following known reverse genetics protocols, Monrad estimates hundreds of thousands worldwide could today reconstruct transmissible influenza. The real question is whether AI will expand this pool by orders of magnitude by teaching more people to complete lab procedures—tasks that once required a PhD final year now might take just weeks of lab training.

28:48 Modest uplift study results lag behind actual model capability
The 2023-24 uplift studies only tested multiple-choice questions, criticized for not capturing real wet lab conditions. A later study—co-sponsored by Active Site and the Frontier Model Forum, with Sentinel also investing—cost over a million dollars and had 150 relative novices complete cell culture, molecular cloning, and virus production tasks in a wet lab, half using state-of-the-art models and half using only internet research. Results showed modest improvements in some tasks but no clear effect on end-to-end processes. Monrad reads this not as reassuring: these studies are slow and expensive; there should be ten such institutions running one quarterly, not annually—otherwise results always lag model iteration speed.

37:15 Tacit knowledge barriers are being actively dismantled by technology
Sonia Ben Ouagrham-Gormley's book on biological weapons barriers once corrected early AI-biosecurity fears that underestimated wet lab know-how. But Monrad says the tide has turned, making people too complacent. These barriers aren't naturally disappearing—"we're actively dismantling them": advances in multimodal systems and computer vision, plus companies deliberately collecting human lab-work videos to train robots or smart glasses that real-time correct pipette angle. This democratizes biology, but Monrad is direct: for many tacit knowledge barriers, it's a death knell.

50:12 Agents can replicate viruses but cannot design entirely new ones
Facing the thought experiment of "misaligned agents deliberately making destructive pathogens," Monrad is specific. For well-studied viruses like influenza, data and protocols are rich—they'll perform well, reaffirming his prior prediction about Active Site results: modest improvements, which he believes will be the last such result. For genuinely novel designs, they'll struggle because biological dimensionality is too high; no dataset can simulate it at once, though he admits we've been "surprised repeatedly." For end-to-end paths requiring zero human involvement, at the time of recording in October 2026, current robotics can't produce a living pathogenic virus no matter how many aligned agents help—but he's hearing more claims that robots may be more of an "LLM-solvable problem" than thought.

58:48 Defenses work by stacking weak signals, not perfect single filters
Sentinel assessed hundreds of control candidates—cell lines, animal models, pipettes, biosafety cabinets—using two criteria: signal-to-noise ratio and concentration (scattered vs. widely available or 3D-printable). Synthetic DNA scores well on both: sequence itself reveals intent, and only ~200 companies globally can synthesize gene-length double-stranded DNA. Most candidate nodes can only be controlled by "prohibition," which would harm both defenders and all life science, making it infeasible. His answer: don't expect one perfect filter. Stack weak signals—an order that diverges from known sequences and serves unclear purpose, plus a flagged model query, plus a suspicious cloud lab application. Individually, none are red flags; together, actionable. KYC evolves into KYA: Know Your Agent.

1:16:07 If I had the button, I would press it
Nathan proposes provocation: frontier model companies controlling trillions of dollars in compute should face concrete biological resilience standards before training continues—a binding "if-then" commitment. Monrad directly agrees. He says he's more confident diagnosing where the world stands on the path to "biological resilience" as a terminal state than what to pause specifically. He flags a common misjudgment: seeing some biodefense investment then thinking training can proceed unchecked—those people haven't calculated what true resilience requires, a decade-plus engineering effort. Subset goals like critical infrastructure or key personnel may move faster.

1:29:36 Desktop DNA synthesizers remain completely unregulated
Monrad believes social incentives diffuse responsibility—for conference chitchat and podcast soundbites on every topic, few go deep on one issue. His team has seen ordering synthetic DNA improve in recent years, with platforms more likely screening and refusing suspicious orders. But this exposes the harder frontier: desktop DNA synthesizers themselves, which need hardware security, sales-end KYC, even geolocation and trade-in buyback plans. Many have mentioned it in papers or tweets; almost no one wakes up daily to solve it. It's truly an unclaimed problem—Sentinel is hiring for it. He also highlights another neglected direction: international diplomacy, hoping Geneva, Beijing, and Singapore's top talent will treat biotech governance as the highest-value work.

item.title: Ultrasound Shattered Rat Liver Tumors; Other Untreated Tumors Vanished
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-05-fromfirstprinc-超声波震碎肝肿瘤-意外让大鼠体内其它肿瘤自行消失/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-05-fromfirstprinc-超声波震碎肝肿瘤-意外让大鼠体内其它肿瘤自行消失/
item.description: In rat liver tumor experiments, 9 of 11 animals with partially ultrasound-destroyed tumors not only showed no metastasis—untreated residual lesions vanished entirely; the mechanism was released antigens activating systemic immune response.
item.content:encoded:
In rat liver tumor experiments, 9 of 11 animals with partially ultrasound-destroyed tumors not only showed no metastasis—untreated residual lesions vanished entirely; the mechanism was released antigens activating systemic immune response.

End-to-end firsthand account of technology development and commercialization; suited for those wanting to understand how deep tech travels from individual labs to billion-dollar companies.

1:06 One Cardiologist's Challenge Forced an Impossible Invention
When Zhen Xu first joined the University of Michigan lab, pediatric cardiologist Ahmad Rudomirsky gave a seminar describing how a patient died on the operating table during congenital heart surgery. He challenged the lab: could you invent a technique that performs true surgery without incisions—he emphasized true surgery because microwave, radiofrequency, and ultrasound heating ablation only cook tissue; they cannot truly remove it, useless to him. This seminar became the origin of what would later be called histotripsy; Zhen Xu decided on the spot to make it her doctoral dissertation, though she had no idea how.

5:26 Cavitation Was Dismissed as Uncontrollable for 50 Years
Cavitation—ultrasound causing bubbles in tissue to expand and contract, mechanically tearing cells—had been observed for nearly 50 years, yet the field believed it could only be controlled by injecting bubbles, otherwise it was random and harmful, like when air in lungs ruptures during imaging. Histotripsy's breakthrough was injecting nothing at all, using only natural nanoscale gas particles in body tissue: these bubbles have surface tension reaching 200 to 300 atmospheres, extremely resistant to cavitation. Precisely because lungs are themselves massive air bubbles, histotripsy still cannot treat lung cancer.

14:54 Silencing the Device Paradoxically Unlocked Tissue Liquefaction
Zhen Xu, with no ultrasound therapy background, followed advisor Charles King's advice to "explore, don't read papers." She found a slaughterhouse in the phone book and went weekly to scavenge discarded pig hearts for experiments, trying every parameter but failing repeatedly, until a colleague complained the equipment was too loud. She did the opposite: raised the pulse repetition frequency above 20 kHz, beyond human hearing—the tradeoff was individual pulse energy actually went down. It was this quieter configuration, chosen for silence not strength, that made pig heart tissue produce a smoke-like phenomenon, creating a hole in one minute—the discovery moment of histotripsy in 2002.

29:27 A Decade Nobody Funded; Only NIH Sustained the Work
After discovering the phenomenon in 2002, Zhen Xu spent nearly a decade—using high-speed cameras to capture microsecond, micrometer-scale bubble activity—before understanding the mechanism. She was blunt: no rational person would fund this kind of work, neither companies nor venture capital would pay for such fundamental research with no visible applications, only NIH funding sustained it. From the initial 2002 discovery to FDA approval for liver cancer treatment in 2023, the journey took 21 years.

38:52 A Student's Personal Tragedy Redirected the Research
The turn to liver cancer came from a request by doctoral student Eli Vlaisavljevich—his mother died of liver cancer when he was young. At the time, the entire field worried that mechanically destroying tumor cells would promote metastasis, so the team designed a rat experiment: intentionally treating only 50–75% of liver tumors, simulating worst-case scenarios, then monitoring metastasis long-term. Control group rats all died within two or three weeks from aggressive hepatocellular carcinoma, but of 11 treated rats, 9 not only saw no tumor spread—even untreated residual tumors vanished completely, nowhere to be found.

42:03 Mechanically Destroying Tumors Unexpectedly Activated Systemic Immunity
The unexpected finding prompted the team to collaborate with tumor immunologist Cliff Cho to investigate, revealing the mechanism: cancer hides itself by suppressing local immune response, while histotripsy converts tumor cells into liquid debris and ruptures cell membranes, releasing previously sequestered tumor antigens into circulation. The body then searches and attacks matching antigens not just at the treatment site but throughout the body—essentially replicating immunotherapy without injecting any drug—also explaining why treating one tumor shrank untreated lesions elsewhere. Zhen Xu emphasized this effect varies by individual, and the team is still exploring how to optimize parameters to amplify it.

47:31 HOPE4LIVER Trial: 90% of Treated Tumors Stayed Gone at One Year
The multicenter clinical trial HOPE4LIVER was the direct basis for FDA approval of histotripsy for liver cancer treatment. Data showed low adverse-event rates; at 30-day follow-up, imaging-confirmed ablation success rate was 96%; at one-year follow-up, local tumor control rate was 90%. Because it's minimally invasive, doctors cannot directly confirm it visually like open surgery, so the entire procedure relies on imaging guidance—doctors outline the tumor on the image, software plans the robotic arm's scanning path accordingly, the doctor confirms and clicks start, and the robot completes treatment automatically, while bubbles from tissue destruction themselves serve as natural ultrasound contrast, letting doctors watch treatment in real time.

1:03:08 $40 Million Federal Funding Became a $3.75 Billion Company
When accepting the Golden Goose Award, Zhen Xu released a set of figures: over roughly 20 years, NIH invested about $40 million funding histotripsy research—early on, no company or investor would fund such fundamental research with no visible applications. Today FDA has approved it for liver cancer treatment, over 5,000 patients have received treatment, HistoSonics is valued at $3.75 billion with 500 employees, and was named by Time magazine as one of the ten most impactful healthcare companies. Her conclusion: federal research funding is the fundamental driver of America's technological innovation leadership.
